blocks.p: Everyone's journey is unique. There's no one-size-fits-all approach to "wellness work." The image in your mind of what change looks like might not match your personal experience, and that's perfectly okay. I invite you to start from scratch and approach your journey with an open mind and a willingness to let things be imperfect, frustrating, and yet hopeful.

While there are generally predictable aspects of change, such as discomfort or frustration, each person's experience will differ. Therefore, it's essential to let go of any preconceived notions about your journey and focus on discovering what works for you. Be open to trying new things, be patient with yourself, and understand that change is a process, not just a result.

Change happens a little at a time. One episode of self-regulation may not be enough. When you research somatic practices in therapy, you may have gotten the impression, and I know I did, that if you do one shake-and-tremble session, you're good to go. Or that you can "reset" or "hack" or "rewire" this or that in a few days and, voila!, you're healed.

But that isn't the case. Not in general and not with the clients I'm working with. The vagal brake is something you continually return to and build. It happens a little at a time, and we want incremental change over a long time. Gradually, it gets stronger and stronger. Moments of distress become fewer and fewer.

And that might be repeated small discharges. You might feel or experience repeated minor releases if you have more freeze energy. And you will then continue to build your safety state along with it. If your system is more shut down, you can expect small doses of empowered, motivated sympathetic activation to fill it over time.
The point is to make progress a little at a time. Things might get difficult before they get easier. This is pretty standard when making any change.

As you practice, you'll notice that you progress clearly at times and take a step back at others. This is normal. Expect it now so it's less jarring when it happens. Change isn't linear. The process is inherently unpredictable and often includes obstacles that can trigger frustration or thoughts of giving up. These obstacles and frustrations are actually a step forward, not back.

It's a catch-22. With more mindfulness and present-moment connection, your body gets the message: "Hey, we're safe." Your body responds, "Okay, cool. Now I can let this stuff out," or "I can climb my Polyvagal ladder now, yippee!" As you keep practicing (which you will), some of that defensive stuff may come up and want to come out. Continue to focus on safety anchoring. That is the absolute priority when it comes to unstucking. The defensive experience is important, but it's secondary to safety.

You should notice increased distress tolerance over time as you practice. Things that were previously triggering will be less so. Eventually, they may not be triggering at all. Things that were stressful before, or the amount of stress you have in your system daily, might go down as you continue to work on your safety anchors and practice safety anchoring. As you unstuck, you will experience more distressing things directly. Doing this and balancing distress with safety will further strengthen your vagal brake and distress tolerance.

Be patient with yourself as you work to get unstuck and achieve your desired life. Unstucking is not a quick fix but an ongoing process that requires dedication and practice, just like building safety. While you may see immediate changes, lasting change happens gradually over time. You're not learning quick fixes. You're learning core self-regulation skills humanity has lost over time.

I don't know how much time you'll need to set aside. I don't. I am going to have to trust you with that. Instead of giving you a specific amount of time, I will encourage you to do more than you did yesterday. More can be tiny.

If you're trying a meditative practice for the first time and have zero experience, 30 seconds is way better than no seconds. I'm not recommending 5 minutes. I'm not recommending 20. I'm just recommending more than yesterday. Do what's easy at first. Find success. Then build on it. You can spend 30 seconds a day for a month, then a minute the next month. If daily feels intimidating, shoot for 3 times per week. Be honest with yourself and choose a schedule that feels easy. That's your starting point.

blocks.why: Thirty seconds is way better than no seconds. This is a short one.

blocks.p: "Pft. I do this stuff for hours at a time! I've been to retreats where all we did was reflect on trauma. My therapist and I meet three times a week to confront my inner pain. I have essential oils, a smart pillow that warms me, a weighted blanket, and…"

If this sounds like you… Slow down. You might be doing too much. (I actually think you are.) Confronting pain doesn't necessarily relieve it. You might be re-traumatizing yourself. If you find this stuff easy, do it differently. I'd rather you spend five minutes deliberately practicing one skill than three hours on "wellness" fill-in-the-blank exercises. Use the other two hours and fifty-five minutes to knit something, play with your grandkids, get a chore done, or watch TV. Take it easy. Seriously.
You're probably busy. So am I. I get it, believe me.

But throughout my life's busyness, I am the constant. Me. I still exist, even when I am busy. I still have the capacity to connect and be intentional, even when I am busy. So being "busy" is not an excuse for not putting in some practice. Saying "I'm too busy" means "I'm not being mindful." You're awake. You're alive. You're just not in the moment, experiencing what you're doing.

You're not too busy. You're just not mindful enough. I get that you have to take the kids to practice. But when you're there, what does the sun feel like on your skin? I know you have to grocery shop, but did you notice how the peaches felt when you were there? And yeah, you need to make a quick run to Target, but can you take a moment to smell one of their candles? In any of these and infinite other moments, you have the opportunity to connect with the present moment and with yourself. All of these are opportunities to ask yourself what it's like to be you.

Once a month on Saturday mornings, I drive down an empty expressway to my office, about 20 minutes away. Every time, the same expressway forces me to stop at every red light without fail. No matter how much I speed up or slow down, I hit every red light. Not only that, but once I come to a complete stop, the light turns green again. Irritation and frustration creep over me, and I think about how much gas I waste every time I need to speed my car back up.

Even in such a situation, there is an opportunity to be mindful. Am I busy? Yes. Am I legitimately frustrated? Yes. But is this an excuse not to be mindful? In a way, heck yes! But also: no, because I'm a busy person and need to squeeze mindfulness into my day in creative, purposeful ways.

My answer to this red light dilemma is this: when I stop at the red lights, I roll the front windows down and feel the air move through my car and across my skin. I stick my hand out the window and feel the air on my arm and my hand. If it's sunny, I also feel the sunlight on my skin. That moment is more than red lights and driving to the office. It's also air and sunlight. If I am too "busy," I lose what else the moment has to offer. So the issue is not that you are too busy; it is that you are not mindful enough within your busyness.

These small moments of mindfulness can go a long, long way. I encourage you to find these moments to connect with safety and to ask yourself what else you feel. This will help you build greater internal awareness and curiosity, setting you up for greater success with unstucking.
I also want you to identify where you can fit in deliberate practice, even if it's just 30 seconds. Here are some potential options:

ul: Right before bed, outside of your bedroom
In the car while your kids are at a practice
First thing in the morning, before everyone else is up

blocks.p: Be consistent in your practice; sporadic efforts are less helpful (though better than nothing). Take this seriously and set the intention to keep practicing right now. Remember, getting unstuck is a process, but you can achieve the change you deserve with dedication, practice, and patience.

None of this (or anything else) will be terribly helpful if you don't have a practice set. Reading and learning are great, but not sufficient. You don't want to just know, right? You want your life to change. Go from knowing to doing. Implement in very small doses as needed, and keep building your practice.

"The journey is more important than the destination" is a well-known saying, and there's a reason for that. While having a goal and working toward it is essential, it's equally important not to become so focused on the result that you forget to appreciate your journey. It's arguably even more critical.

Before getting unstuck and achieving your life-change goals, you first need to take the path. Traveling down your change path will bring obstacles to learn from. For example, as you look inward at your stuck shame, you may discover that anxiety is also present, blocking you from connecting with it. If you remain focused on the shame, you lose the experience of being with anxiety. That step on your journey is still on the path to unstuckness, but it is its own experience.

I guarantee this is going to happen. Other things will present themselves to you. If you neglect them, you're robbing yourself of an opportunity for growth. I also don't expect you to notice everything that comes up for you. For example, as frustration mounts when you can't access safety, you'll probably swear and give up, saying, "Forget this s***!" You'll miss the frustration that needed some attention. You'll focus on the inability to access safety when, really, the frustration is what needs your attention.

Your journey will have ups and downs, and you must experience them all as they arise. Notice what surfaces as it arises, with curiosity, staying grounded in your safety state. This is how you embrace the journey, not just the result.

You exist right here and right now on your journey. If you're focused on the result, you're not in the present moment. Re-anchor in safety and connect with here and now. Once you're connected with here and now, you're back on the journey. If you lose sight of the journey, that's okay. Re-anchor in safety and connect with the present. You will lose access, I promise. You'll also get down on yourself. All of it's okay. It's all part of the process. Tell yourself you're doing your best, give yourself some encouragement, and try again when you're ready.

The great news is that you exist in the present moment, even if you're not consciously connected to it. So every moment of every day is another opportunity to embrace your present-moment experience, re-anchor in safety, and connect with yourself. Just like this present moment. And in this one. And just like all the ones to follow. In each of these present moments, you can ask yourself, "What's it like to be me?"

blocks.prompt: What mindfulness or self-regulation practices are you doing now that are more than yesterday? If nothing yet, what's one small, easy step you could add to your day?
Where can you fit in thirty seconds of mindfulness?
When are you the most regulated, and can enhance it?
